cards.title: Set up a persistent AI project for SEO and product research
cards.summary: Use a dedicated AI project (not a single chat) to hold your business brief and research files so long ecommerce SEO workflows don't lose context.
cards.use_when: Starting any multi-step keyword, content or AI-visibility project for a store and you plan to paste many research files over several sessions.
steps: Create a new project/workspace in your AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude or similar) rather than running everything in one chat thread. The source's rationale: a single chat has a limited context window, so the AI gradually forgets your earlier business information; a project retains the files you add.
Generate a business brief first: paste a prompt or your store URL and answer the questions about what you sell, who you sell to and where. Save the output as a text file.
Add that brief file as a source inside the project so every later prompt (keyword clustering, category copy, PDP content) inherits the correct catalog and positioning context.
Add each new research artifact to the project as you produce it — keyword clusters, competitor keyword exports, sitemap breakdowns — instead of re-explaining them in chat.
Reuse the same project for content generation and AI-citation work so market, audience and product terminology stay consistent across pages.
caveats: Context limits and project features in AI tools change; verify the current interface.
The source recommends this for service businesses; for ecommerce the brief should capture catalog, categories, target buyer and fulfillment areas, not just services.

cards.title: Understand GEO and the two new AI-visibility KPIs
cards.summary: Generative Engine Optimization is the practice of getting your brand into AI-generated answers, measured by citations and brand mentions rather than clicks alone.
cards.use_when: Deciding what success looks like for a store's presence in ChatGPT, AI overviews or Perplexity, and choosing metrics to track alongside organic traffic.
steps: Define the category: generative engines (ChatGPT, Google AI overviews, Perplexity) produce an answer instead of sending the user to a blue link, so the goal shifts from ranking-and-clicking to being included in the generated answer.

Track two new KPIs alongside organic traffic and conversion: (1) citations — the AI uses your content to build its answer; (2) mentions — the AI names your brand or business. These are distinct events and both matter.

Map your existing pages against likely AI questions in your niche (e.g. 'best [product category] for X', 'is [product] worth it') and check whether your content is being cited or your brand mentioned.
Keep purchase conversion and revenue as the ultimate commercial outcome; citations and mentions are intermediate visibility metrics, not sales metrics.

Note the source's position that GEO is the only new acronym worth adopting because it is the one appearing in peer-reviewed work; treat other labels (AEO, LLM SEO) as synonyms rather than separate disciplines.
caveats: The source describes GEO as built on top of traditional SEO — it estimates classic SEO still accounts for roughly 80% of the work; this is the presenter's heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
Citation and mention tracking tools and AI engine behavior change frequently.

cards.title: Discard three common GEO myths before planning store content
cards.summary: Google penalizes thin content not AI-written content, the AI model you use is not a ranking factor, and traditional SEO still underpins AI visibility.
cards.use_when: When a stakeholder or agency argues for or against using AI to produce store product and category content.
steps: Myth 1 — 'Google penalizes AI content.' The source's correction: Google penalizes thin, spammy, no-value content regardless of who or what wrote it. A carefully written AI-assisted product page can rank; a low-effort human-written one will not. Base your quality bar on usefulness, not on authorship.

Myth 2 — 'Picking the right model improves rankings.' The source states the AI model is not and never was a ranking factor, and that current models are more than capable for SEO/SEO-adjacent writing. Use the AI tool you already pay for rather than switching.

Myth 3 — 'AI changed everything; old rules are dead.' The source argues AI search is built on traditional SEO, so solid classic on-page work still delivers most of the GEO benefit. Treat AI-specific techniques as an addition to, not a replacement for, fundamentals.

Practical implication for ecommerce: continue investing in accurate descriptions, specifications, structured data and genuinely helpful buying guidance, and add extractable answer formats on top rather than instead.
caveats: These are the presenter's framings of Google's position; Google's guidance and enforcement evolve, so verify current official statements before making irreversible content decisions.
AI-detector tools are dismissed by the source as unreliable and not a planning input.

cards.title: Translate customer language into keyword research, not expert terminology
cards.summary: Research the words buyers actually type, which often differ from industry jargon, and split the task into transactional and informational keywords.
cards.use_when: Choosing which search terms a product, category or landing page should target before writing copy or building pages.
steps: List the terms your team uses internally and then list what a first-time buyer would type. The source's example: installers call it 'EVSE installation', customers search 'Tesla charger installation' — the customer phrasing wins because that is the query with demand.

Separate keywords into two buckets the source uses: transactional (buying intent, e.g. 'home EV charger installation' — the shopper wants the product now) and informational (research intent, e.g. 'EV charger installation cost' — the shopper is still deciding).
Start transactional research from your own catalog: enumerate every product, category and service-equivalent page you intend to have, then check search volume and difficulty for each.
Then mine informational queries around the same seed terms — these become blog posts, buying guides and FAQ content that support the commercial pages.
Save every candidate keyword into a planner/spreadsheet and cluster them by seed topic so you can see which page each term belongs to.
Do this per product line or category rather than once for the whole store, so each page gets its own dedicated target.
caveats: The source stresses that third-party SEO tools only give direction — volume and difficulty numbers are estimates, not truth.
Location and language settings materially change results; set the market you actually sell into.

cards.title: Run transactional keyword research and cluster it by page
cards.summary: Take each core commercial term through an SEO tool's overview and suggestions, save the related terms and cluster them so one page owns each topic.
cards.use_when: Building or restructuring category and product landing pages, and deciding which terms each commercial page should target.
steps: Pick a seed transactional term for a category or product (e.g. 'home EV charger installation') and pull its overview: monthly search volume, difficulty score, and cost-per-click. High CPC suggests commercial value worth targeting.

Save the seed term to a planner, then open the tool's suggestions/related-keywords view to surface adjacent query variants — the source calls these secondary or LSI keywords that search and AI engines expect to see together.

While scanning suggestions, note brand-specific and audience-specific variants (e.g. 'Tesla charger installation', 'BMW EV charger', 'EV charger for businesses'), because these can justify dedicated sub-pages if they show volume.
Watch for modifiers that signal a separate page: costs, rebates, requirements, commercial vs residential. If a variant has its own demand, plan a page rather than cramming it into the main one.
Save every relevant term to the planner, then create a cluster around the seed keyword so the tool groups them and shows total cluster volume.
Export the cluster as CSV and load it into your AI project, then repeat the whole sequence for each of your other categories/services so every commercial page has its own keyword set.
caveats: Cluster volume totals are tool estimates — treat as directional, not as guaranteed traffic.
The presenter's own tool (Datawise) is used in the demo and is disclosed as his paid product; equivalent workflow exists in Ahrefs, Semrush or similar tools.

cards.title: Mine People-Also-Ask questions for buying-guide content
cards.summary: Pull PAA questions at depth around a core term and turn them into FAQ and guide content that answers real pre-purchase doubts.
cards.use_when: Planning buying guides, FAQ blocks and supporting content that feeds shoppers toward your commercial pages.
steps: Take a core transactional term and run a People-Also-Ask search in your SEO tool with search depth set high (the demo uses depth 3) to surface related questions across the market.
Expand each PAA entry — clicking through reveals subsequent nested questions — to build a fuller list; the demo returned over 140 questions for one term.

Manually review the list rather than trusting the AI blindly; select the questions that genuinely apply to what you sell and that a real buyer would ask (price, suitability, operating cost, whether a standard installer/consumer option works).
Export the selected questions as CSV and add them to your AI project with context, so later content prompts can address them directly.

Use these questions as FAQ blocks on commercial pages (the source suggests keeping commercial-page FAQs short, no more than about five, to preserve the page's transactional focus) and as full buying-guide topics where enough depth exists.
Repeat for each main category so each buying guide is grounded in questions real shoppers ask around that specific product.
caveats: PAA lists are noisy; the source explicitly recommends human review over bulk acceptance.
Question availability varies by market and language.

cards.title: Answer fan-out queries to win AI citations
cards.summary: Fan-out queries are the internal follow-up questions an AI asks itself when handling a broad prompt; answering them in your content raises citation chances.
cards.use_when: Writing guide, FAQ or PDP content aimed at being cited by ChatGPT, AI overviews or Perplexity for a broad category question.
steps: Understand the mechanic: when a shopper asks an AI a broad question (e.g. 'should I install an EV charger at home?'), the engine decomposes it into sub-questions — costs, permits, local availability — researches each, then synthesizes an answer. Those sub-questions are the fan-out queries.

Find them using a tool that exposes fan-out data (the demo uses a fan-out queries view seeded with a core term; the source notes this data is currently US/English-only, so even non-US sellers can use it preemptively).
Filter hard: the demo returned ~195 queries for one seed and many were irrelevant to the business, so select only the ones your products actually answer.
Fold the selected fan-out questions into your content as headings with direct answers, alongside the People-Also-Ask questions — the source expects heavy overlap between the two lists.
Expect some queries to sit at the informational top of your editorial plan and others to belong on commercial pages as FAQ entries; route each to the appropriate page type.
Treat this as the GEO-specific layer on top of the keyword research you already did, and re-check periodically because fan-out data and coverage change.
caveats: Fan-out query data is described as new and limited to US English at time of recording; coverage may expand.
The source flags that fan-out lists contain irrelevant entries that must be discarded manually.

cards.title: Do a four-part competitor analysis to plan your page architecture
cards.summary: Study competitors' ranking keywords, winning pages, sitemap structure and backlink profile to decide how much content and how many pages your store needs.
cards.use_when: Planning a category/blog structure for a new store or a new product line, or diagnosing why competitors outrank you.
steps: Pick real competitors: search your main commercial term, exclude sponsored results, and also ask an AI assistant (outside your project) who it recommends for the query to see who is being cited. Choose two to five root domains.
Run a domain comparison in an SEO tool to see total ranking keywords, traffic estimates and keyword value. Identify the competitor with the most ranking keywords and examine them in depth.

Open their ranked keyword list and look at which URLs win. In the source's example, the leader ranked mostly with blog posts plus dedicated location pages — that revealed the page types needed to compete.

Fetch their sitemap (domain/sitemap.xml), paste it into your AI project and ask for it to be categorized into commercial pages, location pages and blog posts as CSV, so you can see the structural scale you must match.

Check their backlinks tab: count backlinks and referring domains, review which links exist (directory/business listings, press, associations) and note the spam score. This tells you whether off-page work will be needed if on-page alone can't close the gap.

Convert findings into your own page count and content plan: match the page types that are working, plan to execute them better, and flag backlinking as a later phase rather than an immediate requirement.
caveats: The source treats this as a flexible, judgment-based process, not a fixed checklist — the right depth changes with the market.
Competitor tools give estimates; a high spam score is described as a good sign (low spam) but you should interpret link quality yourself.

cards.title: Build one dedicated page per product or service
cards.summary: Splitting every offering onto its own page is the single most important structural decision for ranking commercial pages.
cards.use_when: Designing category, product or service page structure, especially when tempted to consolidate several offerings onto one page.
steps: Apply the source's rule: one page per service/product line, not one page listing everything. The presenter calls cramming everything onto one page the number-one mistake he sees.
Create a hub page for the broader offering and dedicated pages beneath it for each specific product/service, so each page can own its own keyword and intent.
Let the keyword research determine how many pages you need — the number of pages you build should follow demand, not convenience.
Build one page to a checklist you're happy with, then reuse it as a template for the others, changing the content for each target rather than duplicating.
Sequence this work initially in one page type (e.g. your most valuable category) before scaling across the catalog, so the template is proven before replication.
caveats: The source's example is a service business; the structural principle (separate pages per distinct offering and target keyword) is what transfers to ecommerce categories and product lines.
A dedicated page needs enough distinct search demand to justify it — confirm volume per offering first.

cards.title: Apply the 2-second rule to commercial page first folds
cards.summary: Within two seconds of landing, a visitor must know what you offer, where you offer it, and what to do next.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing the above-the-fold area of a product, category, service or payment landing page.
steps: Check three things in the first fold, without scrolling: (1) what you do/sell, (2) where you do/sell it (for local businesses — location/page relevance), (3) the next action you want the visitor to take.

Write a plain, direct headline rather than a tagline. The source contrasts an ambiguous example ('You're spending the money. You just can't see what it's doing...') with a clear one: 'Professional home EV charger installation in Austin. Get a free quote.'

Make the H1 state exactly what the page offers and answer the implicit question 'can you do this for me / is this the thing I want?' The source treats one H1 per page as a technical requirement (see the structured-data card).
Place a primary call to action above the fold — a prominent button matching the outcome the visitor wants (get a quote, add to cart, shop the range).
Save creative taglines and brand flourish for further down the page or other placements; keep the first fold unambiguous because that is where bounce decisions are made.
caveats: The 2-second rule is the presenter's heuristic for commercial pages, not a measured standard.
What 'where' means differs online vs local; for pure ecommerce, location may be replaced by delivery/return terms or product fit rather than geography.

cards.title: Run a commercial-page checklist: intent, one keyword, schema, design, specifics
cards.summary: Five checks determine whether a product or service page will perform, starting with search-intent match and including structured data and evidence.
cards.use_when: Finalising a new category, product or service page before publishing.
steps: Intent match: confirm the page answers the searcher's intent — a transactional query needs a page where the product can be bought or requested, not an article about the topic.
One main keyword per page: assign a single primary target and use secondary/related terms naturally through subheadings and body copy rather than spreading several primaries across one page.

Schema: add appropriate structured data (service/product schema as applicable) so search engines understand exactly what the page contains. The source says you can rank without it but you're giving up an advantage; SEO plugins often insert it, but validate the output rather than assuming.

Conversion-friendly design and evidence: prefer real photos of the actual work/product over stock imagery where possible, be specific about prices, include reviews (ideally reviews mentioning that specific product/service), and add a how-it-works section.

Body structure: use additional H2/H3s for related keywords, and include a short FAQ of the most-asked questions for that specific offering — the source advises keeping commercial-page FAQs to no more than about five so the page stays transactional.

Use the first fold as the priority: pass the 2-second rule (what/where/next action), keep the headline plain, keep H1 exact, and place a primary CTA above the fold. If roughly 90% of these boxes are ticked, the source considers the page in good shape.
caveats: The source deliberately avoids prescribing a word count — length should follow what the page needs, not a target.
Blog/informational content should be kept off commercial pages beyond a short FAQ to avoid diluting transactional focus.
Structured-data support and plugin behavior change; verify with a current validator.

cards.title: Enforce one H1 per page and validate structured data
cards.summary: Every page should carry exactly one H1 that states the offering, with H2–H4 for everything else, plus verified structured data.
cards.use_when: Auditing on-page technical setup across a store's templates, especially after theme changes or migrations.
steps: Ensure exactly one H1 per page — the source presents this as a technical mandate to avoid confusing Google. Additional headings should be H2, H3, H4 and so on.

Watch platform defaults: the source notes that on some themes (he cites Shopify's Dawn theme) the homepage H1 is typically the logo, which means the homepage H1 may not be describing your offering. Check and adjust.
Make the H1 state exactly what the page offers so both users and crawlers recognise the page topic quickly.

Inspect the title tag, meta description, heading hierarchy and structured data using a browser extension (the source demonstrates a free Chrome extension for on-page inspection; verify the current tool).

Confirm the most important schema for the page type is present — for a service/commercial page the source highlights service schema as the key one. Many SEO plugins insert schema automatically, but you must validate it, not assume it.
Re-run the audit after any theme, template or plugin change, since these can alter headings and schema.
caveats: Platform default behaviour (e.g. logo as homepage H1) varies by theme and version — check your own store rather than assuming.
Plugins are described as doing a reasonable job but not a guaranteed-correct one; validation is the control step.

cards.title: Write content capsules so AI engines can extract clean answers
cards.summary: Place a short, self-contained 20–25 word answer directly under each question heading so AI engines can lift it as a citation.
cards.use_when: Writing buying guides, blog posts and FAQ sections on product or category pages aimed at AI citations.
steps: Structure each section as a question heading (H2) followed immediately by a direct answer. The capsule must make sense on its own, without the surrounding article.

Answer immediately — no warm-up sentences. Example from the source: heading 'How much does it cost to install an EV charger at home?' is answered directly with the price range, not with 'in the ever-evolving world of EV chargers...'.
Keep the capsule around 20–25 words. Going over 50 words is acceptable if the answer genuinely requires detail, but brevity is the default.
Target roughly 60–70% of the piece written in capsule form. The remaining 30–40% can be freer prose (process explanations, narrative sections) so the article still reads well to humans.
Do not put links inside the capsule itself — keep it clean for extraction. Put citations in the surrounding text instead.

Cite sources for factual statements, especially any numbers, by linking a contextual keyword to the origin. The source argues that citing sources increases trust and is important for AI engines, and that fear of losing traffic to citations signals a content problem, not a linking problem.

Add first-hand experience wherever possible — the source describes lived experience as the element AI engines can't yet replicate. Experience can be simple ('we tried X and got Y, so do/don't do Z'), not only decades of credentials.
Use the checklist/structure the source provides (structure, sourcing, coverage, on-page, things to avoid) and expect the workflow to become habitual after three or four pieces.
caveats: The 60–70% capsule proportion and 20–25 word target are the source's working heuristics, not measured thresholds.
The technique is described as supported by peer-reviewed study, but results will vary by topic and engine.

cards.title: Prompt an AI to draft capsule-style content from your keyword research
cards.summary: Feed the AI your brief, topic, audience and selected keywords to produce a structured capsule-format draft with sources and first-hand experience slots.
cards.use_when: Drafting buying guides, comparison posts or FAQ-driven blog content that should be extractable by AI engines.
steps: Inside your project, paste a content prompt that instructs the AI to use the content-capsule technique, and supply three inputs: the topic, the audience, and the goal.

Choose the topic from your keyword planner — the source notes you can take a People-Also-Ask or fan-out question as the main topic with related questions as subheadings, and that the tooling offers a content map where one query becomes the post topic and others become sections.
Describe the audience specifically (e.g. 'homeowners in Dallas, Texas who just bought an EV') — the more you know about the audience, the more useful the prompt output.

Let the AI run its research phase: it should surface top-ranking pages for the term and a set of high-quality sources to cite (in the demo these skew toward government sites). Review the sources rather than accepting them blind.
Approve the proposed structure — headings, where capsules go, a table or two, and an FAQ section at the end. Ask for variants (tables, differentiators) to make the content less uniform.
Before requesting the first draft, insert proprietary detail the AI cannot know ('when we did X we found problem Y') so experience and specificity are baked in.
Pull the first draft, then edit — the source treats the AI output as a first draft and warns against trusting it blindly.
caveats: AI models sometimes over-ask clarifying questions; the source suggests capping those if the list gets too long.
Prompts and tool interfaces change, so verify the current prompt template and features.
Do not let cited sources or claims stand unchecked — the source repeatedly advises human review.

cards.title: Build a content map that routes keywords to the right page type
cards.summary: Use your cluster data to assign each keyword to a commercial page, FAQ, or full article, so supporting content feeds the money pages.
cards.use_when: Planning an editorial calendar or deciding whether a keyword deserves its own page, a section, or an FAQ entry.
steps: Work from the planner/cluster view of your saved keywords, segmented into transactional and informational groups.
Identify which queries deserve an entire article. In the source's tooling, a content map flags one query as the post topic and related queries as the subheadings to answer within it.
Route commercial-intent keywords to money pages — one primary keyword per page — and keep informational content off those pages beyond a short FAQ.
Route informational keyword groups to buying guides or explainer posts written in capsule style, since these are the pages most likely to be cited by AI engines.

Keep the relationship visible: supporting articles should link contextually to the relevant product/category page, because the article's job is to capture research-stage demand and hand it to the commercial page.
Revisit the map as clusters grow, so a section that gains enough demand can be promoted into its own page.
caveats: The source's routing logic is a lightweight two-bucket model (transactional vs informational); more complex intent taxonomies exist and may be needed on large catalogs.
Tool features for content maps change; the principle is separable from any one product.

cards.title: Use citations and first-hand experience as AI-trust signals
cards.summary: Backing claims with sources and adding lived experience to your content increases trust with readers and citation likelihood with AI engines.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing any buying guide, comparison page or product explanation where factual claims and prices are stated.
steps: Whenever you state a number or factual claim, link a relevant contextual word to the origin of that information. The source frames this as at least as important as writing well.

Answer the fear that outbound links leak traffic by improving the content instead — the presenter argues that if a reader leaves because you showed a source, the content wasn't strong enough to hold them.

Add first-hand experience in a form AI can't reproduce: outcomes and specific observations from actually using or selling the product ('we tried X and got Y'). This does not require years of credentials — a single documented result counts.
Give the AI these experience details explicitly in your prompt, because it cannot invent your operational knowledge.
Distinguish this from generic marketing claims: the goal is verifiable specificity that a reader (and an engine) can trust.
caveats: This is the source's argument about trust and citation behaviour, not a measured ranking guarantee.
Citations must be relevant and accurate; a low-quality source undermines the intent.

cards.title: Iterate to a proven page template before scaling across the catalog
cards.summary: Perfect one commercial page against the checklist, then replicate the structure across other offerings and page types.
cards.use_when: Scaling a store's page production after the first category or service page performs structurally well.
steps: Build one page against the full checklist — intent match, single main keyword, schema, conversion-friendly design, 2-second-rule first fold, short FAQ, real imagery, specific pricing.

Review it critically before replicating: check the first fold, headings, schema validity and keyword placement. The source notes that fresh eyes (a second reviewer) catch what the original builder misses.
Treat that page as a structural template, not a content template — every page keeps the framework but gets its own copy, keywords and evidence.
Apply the same discipline to content pages: once one capsule-style article performs, reuse the prompt structure and section rhythm for other topics.
Track results and revisit structure if performance lags, since the source recommends validating before full rollout and being willing to change the structure by market and competitor landscape.
caveats: The source warns against copy-pasting identical content across pages — only the structure should repeat.
No specific rollout volume or timeline is given; pace depends on catalog size and resources.
